title: How to Choose the Right Engagement Ring Setting
excerpt: Solitaire, halo or bezel: how each setting frames the stone, and what suits everyday wear.

image.alt: A woman resting her hand on her cheek, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: A setting holds the center stone and shapes the whole look of the ring. Before you choose a style, think about how you use your hands: a ring worn through work, sport and travel needs a different setting from one worn mostly for special occasions.
Prongs grip the stone with small metal claws and let in the most light. A bezel wraps the stone in a thin rim of metal, which protects its edge and sits smoothly against clothing.

A halo circles the center stone with smaller diamonds, adding brightness and making it look larger. Pavé lines the band with small diamonds. Side-stone and three-stone settings flank the center stone with accents for a fuller look.
Choose the setting that suits your life first and your style second. A simple solitaire is timeless; a halo or pavé band adds sparkle. Try a few on before you decide.

featuredImage.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

title: A Simple Routine for Keeping Jewelry Bright
excerpt: A few minutes a week keeps diamonds and gold shining: what to use, what to avoid and when to see a jeweler.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Soak gold and diamond pieces in warm water with a drop of mild soap, brush gently with a soft toothbrush, rinse and pat dry. Lotion and everyday dust dull a diamond quickly, so a little cleaning makes a visible difference.
Keep jewelry away from bleach, chlorine and abrasive cleaners. Softer and treated gemstones, pearls and emeralds among them, need only a damp cloth.
Have rings checked from time to time for worn prongs or loose stones, especially pieces you wear every day. A jeweler can also polish away fine scratches and renew a white gold finish.
Put jewelry on last and take it off first, store pieces apart, and clean them little and often.

featuredImage.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

title: Lab-Grown or Natural: What Sets Them Apart
excerpt: Both are real diamonds. Here is how they differ in origin, price and how they are graded.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Lab-grown and natural diamonds share the same chemical composition, crystal structure, hardness and sparkle. To the eye they are the same; telling them apart takes specialized laboratory equipment.

Natural diamonds formed deep in the earth over a very long time. Lab-grown diamonds are created in a laboratory, by high pressure and high temperature or by chemical vapor deposition, processes that recreate the conditions in which diamonds form.

Grading reports for both state the origin, and some laboratories describe a lab-grown diamond’s quality on a different scale, so check which scale a report uses. Prices differ too, so compare a lab-grown and a natural diamond of similar size and quality to see what each offers within your budget.
There is no wrong choice. Decide whether natural origin or size and grade matters more to you, and choose the diamond you love.

featuredImage.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

title: How to Layer Necklaces
excerpt: Start with one piece you love, then build around it: lengths, weights and textures for a layered look that stays put.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

hero.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

featuredImage.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Start With One Piece You Love

The easiest layered looks are built around a single favorite: a pendant you wear every day, a fine chain with a little sparkle, or a bolder link. Decide which piece is the star, then choose the others to frame it rather than compete with it.
Two or three necklaces are plenty to begin with. Lay them out on a flat surface before you put them on, so you can see how the lengths and textures work together.

A simple chain close to the neck makes a good base. Fine cable and paperclip chains are versatile because they sit flat and suit almost any neckline. From there, each layer should hang a little lower than the one above, with enough space between them that each can be seen on its own. Keep the finest chain highest and the heaviest lowest, so the weight sits naturally and the layers don’t pull on one another.

image.alt: A woman wearing layered gold necklaces, one set with a green stone

body.text: Add Contrast in Length and Texture

Pair a delicate chain with a bolder one, or a plain chain with a pendant, so the eye moves from one to the next. Mixing textures, such as a smooth chain beside a link chain, adds interest without adding more pieces.

The same thinking works on your hands. An engagement ring or a favorite statement ring is the anchor; slim bands on either side frame it. Stacks look best when the rings share something, whether a metal, a shape or a level of sparkle.

Yellow, white and rose gold can be worn together. Repeat each metal at least twice, on the neck or the hands, so the mix looks deliberate, and use a piece that combines metals to tie the look together.

body.label: A simple three-ring stack:
items: A plain band below your center ring, to protect it and give it a base.
Your center ring, the piece the stack is built around.
A slim pavé or textured band above it, to add sparkle without crowding.

body.text: Necklace lengths have traditional names. Knowing them makes it easier to plan layers that fall at different points, so each necklace has its own space.

cells: At the base of the neck
At the top of the chest

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Layers tangle less when the chains differ in weight and length. A necklace spacer or a single multi-strand piece can keep them apart. Take layered necklaces off one at a time and store them separately, with the clasps fastened.
There are no strict rules to layering. Start with one piece you love, give every layer its own space, and repeat a metal or a shape so the whole look holds together. Then wear what feels like you.

title: Sapphires Beyond Blue
excerpt: Pink, yellow, green and more: the many colors of sapphire, and why it suits a ring worn every day.

image.alt: A woman resting her hand on her cheek, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Sapphire is the mineral corundum, and while blue is its best-known color, it also comes in pink, yellow, orange, purple, green and colorless white. Red corundum has its own name: ruby.
Look for even color that stays rich in different light. Many sapphires are heated to improve their color, a common and stable treatment that should be disclosed.
At 9 on the Mohs scale, sapphire is one of the hardest gemstones, which makes it a lasting choice for an engagement ring or a band you never take off.
If you love color, a sapphire is a durable way to wear it every day.

featuredImage.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

title: Stacking Rings: Mixing Metals and Shapes
excerpt: Simple rules for pairing bands with your engagement ring, from contrast metals to matching curves.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

hero.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: Every stack needs a center: an engagement ring, a statement ring or a favorite band. Build outward from it with slimmer rings so it keeps its place.
Round stones sit easily with round-edged bands; emerald and princess cuts suit straight lines. Curved bands follow pear, marquise and oval stones closely.
Yellow, white and rose gold work together when each appears more than once. A two-tone ring or a band in a second metal ties the mix together.
Start with three rings, add one at a time, and stop when the stack still feels comfortable to wear.

featuredImage.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

title: Choosing a Wedding Band to Match Your Engagement Ring
excerpt: Flush, curved or contrasting: how to find a band that sits well beside your engagement ring.

image.alt: A woman resting her hand on her cheek, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring and a band

body.text: Bring your engagement ring when you try bands. If its setting sits above the band, a straight band can sit flush beside it. If the center stone or a halo sits low, a curved or notched band follows its shape and closes the gap.
A band about as wide as your engagement ring’s shank looks balanced. A slimmer band lets the engagement ring lead; a wider one makes a bolder pair.

Choose the same metal and finish for a matched set, or contrast them, yellow gold beside platinum or a brushed band beside a polished ring, for a modern look. Diamond bands add sparkle; plain bands let the center stone stand out.
Wear the two rings together for a few minutes before you decide. The right band feels comfortable and looks like it belongs.

featuredImage.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring and a band

title: Carat Weight and Diamond Size
excerpt: Carat is weight, not size. How weight translates to what you see, and why shape and cut change it.
subtitle: Carat is weight, not size: how it translates to what you see on the hand.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring and a band

body.text: A carat is a unit of weight equal to 0.2 grams, divided into 100 points. A half-carat diamond is a 50-point diamond. Weight is the most precise of the 4Cs, measured to the hundredth of a carat, but it doesn’t tell you directly how large a diamond will look.

Face-up size depends on how the weight is distributed. A well-cut round diamond keeps its weight where it can be seen, while a deep stone hides weight below the girdle. Elongated shapes such as oval, marquise and pear spread their weight over a longer outline, so they tend to look larger than a round diamond of the same weight.
The same diamond looks larger on a slender finger than on a wider one, and a thin band or a halo can make the center stone look bigger still. Try a few weights on your own hand before you decide.

Diamonds are often cut to reach popular weights, such as the half and whole carat, and a stone just below one of these looks almost the same on the hand. If you want the look of a full carat, a well-cut diamond just under it gives nearly the same face-up size; it is the cut, more than the last few points, that decides how large and bright it looks.
A slim band, a halo of small diamonds or a white metal setting can all make a center stone look larger, while a wide band or heavy prongs make it look smaller by comparison.

title: Diamond Clarity, Explained
excerpt: Inclusions, blemishes and the clarity scale, and what “eye-clean” means.
subtitle: Inclusions, blemishes and the clarity scale, and what “eye-clean” means.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: Most diamonds contain tiny features formed as they grew: crystals, feathers, clouds and needles inside the stone, called inclusions, and small marks on the surface, called blemishes. Clarity grades describe how visible they are under 10x magnification.

GIA uses eleven grades in six groups: Flawless (FL), Internally Flawless (IF), Very Very Slightly Included (VVS1, VVS2), Very Slightly Included (VS1, VS2), Slightly Included (SI1, SI2) and Included (I1, I2, I3). The position of an inclusion matters too: one near the center of the table is easier to see than one near the edge.

An eye-clean diamond shows no inclusions to the unaided eye at a normal viewing distance. Many VS and some SI diamonds are eye-clean, so you rarely need the highest grades for a stone that looks clean on the hand. Step cuts like emerald and Asscher are the exception: their open facets show more, so aim higher with those shapes.

Crystals are tiny minerals trapped inside the diamond as it grew; some are colorless, others dark. Feathers are small breaks within the stone that can look white or reflective. Clouds are groups of tiny pinpoints that, when dense, can make a diamond look slightly hazy. Needles are thin, long crystals. Most are harmless, but a large feather that reaches the surface, especially near a prong or the girdle, is worth asking a jeweler about, because it can make that area more vulnerable to a hard knock.

Full grading reports usually include a plot: a map of the diamond’s main inclusions, drawn with symbols explained in a key. It helps you match the report to the stone and see where the characteristics that set its grade lie.

title: Diamond Color, From D to Z
excerpt: How the color scale works, where differences become visible, and how your metal changes what you see.
subtitle: How the color scale works, and how your metal changes what you see.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: White diamonds are graded on a scale that runs from D, which is colorless, to Z, which has a light yellow or brown tint. Graders compare each diamond face down against master stones under controlled lighting, because color is easiest to judge from the side.

image.alt: A colorless round diamond
A near colorless round diamond with a hint of warmth
A round diamond with a faint yellow tint

body.text: Once a diamond is face up and set, small color differences are much harder to see. White gold and platinum show a diamond’s own color most honestly, so colorless and high near-colorless grades suit them. Yellow and rose gold reflect warm tones into the stone, so a slight warmth in the diamond is less noticeable in them.

Some diamonds glow, usually blue, under ultraviolet light. Fluorescence is usually listed on grading reports. In most diamonds it has no visible effect in daylight; in a few, strong fluorescence can make the stone look slightly hazy, so it is worth seeing a strongly fluorescent diamond before you choose it.

Decide on the metal first, then the grade. In white gold or platinum, a G or H diamond usually looks white face up. In yellow or rose gold, an I or J diamond often looks white against the metal. Larger diamonds and step cuts such as emerald and Asscher show color more readily than small or brilliant-cut stones, so a grade higher can be worth it for them. Above all, compare diamonds side by side in the setting you have in mind, rather than relying on the letter alone.

title: How Cut Shapes a Diamond’s Sparkle
excerpt: Why proportions, symmetry and polish matter more to sparkle than any other grade, and what to check on a report.
subtitle: Proportions, symmetry and polish, and why cut matters more to sparkle than any other grade.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring and a band

body.text: A diamond’s cut controls how light travels through it. When the angles are right, light bounces from facet to facet and returns through the top as brightness, fire and sparkle. When they are off, light leaks out of the sides or bottom and the stone looks dull, whatever its color or clarity.

GIA grades the cut of round brilliant diamonds from Excellent through Very Good, Good and Fair to Poor. The grade weighs the diamond’s proportions, such as table size, crown angle and pavilion depth, together with its symmetry and polish. Fancy shapes such as ovals and pears don’t receive a GIA cut grade, so judge them by eye and by their symmetry and polish grades.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.caption: Fancy shapes are judged by eye: look for even brightness from end to end.

body.text: Shape describes a diamond’s outline: round, oval, emerald and so on. Cut describes how well that shape has been faceted. Every shape can be cut well or poorly, so choose the shape you love first, then look for the best cut within it.

Look at the diamond face up under ordinary light. A well-cut stone looks evenly bright, with crisp contrast between light and dark areas. Large dark patches in the center, or a window you can see through, suggest light is escaping.

Symmetry describes how precisely the facets are shaped, aligned and meet, and polish how smooth their surfaces are. Both are graded on the report, from Excellent to Poor. Small differences rarely show to the eye, but poor symmetry can send light out at the wrong angles and dull a stone’s sparkle. For a round diamond, the cut grade already takes symmetry and polish into account. For fancy shapes, which have no cut grade, Excellent or Very Good symmetry and polish are a good sign.

title: Diamond Shapes
excerpt: From round brilliant to emerald cut: how each shape plays with light, and what to look for in it.
subtitle: How each shape plays with light, and what to look for in it.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Brilliant cuts use many triangular and kite-shaped facets to make the most of sparkle. The round brilliant is the classic, and the shape whose cut is graded most precisely. Oval, cushion, princess, radiant, pear, marquise and heart are brilliant-style cuts too, each with its own outline.

Elongated shapes are described by their length-to-width ratio. A higher ratio makes an oval or pear look longer and slimmer; a lower one makes it rounder. There is no right ratio, only the outline you prefer. In elongated brilliants, look out for a bow-tie: a dark band across the center that some stones show more than others.

Emerald and Asscher cuts have long, parallel facets arranged like steps. Rather than many small flashes, they show broad flashes of light and a calm, hall-of-mirrors look. Their open facets reveal more of a diamond’s clarity and color, so a higher clarity and color grade is often worth it for a step cut.

Start with the shape you are drawn to, then think about how it suits your hand and the setting. Elongated shapes, such as oval, pear and marquise, can make fingers look longer and tend to look larger for their weight. Round and cushion shapes are classic and versatile. Shapes with points, such as pear, marquise, princess and heart, are best protected by a prong or a V-shaped tip over each point, since a point can chip with a hard knock. If you will wear a band beside your ring, try the two together, as some outlines sit more neatly beside a band than others.

title: Emeralds
excerpt: The green variety of beryl: why inclusions are expected, how emeralds are treated, and how to care for them.
subtitle: Why inclusions are expected, and how to care for an emerald.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Emerald is the green variety of the mineral beryl, colored by traces of chromium and vanadium. Its color is valued above all: a rich, even green with good transparency.
Inclusions Are Part of the Stone

Almost all emeralds contain inclusions, sometimes called a jardin, French for garden. They are expected, and judged more gently than in diamonds. Many emeralds are treated with oil or resin to make fine fissures less visible, a common and widely accepted practice.

Emerald is 7.5 to 8 on the Mohs scale, but inclusions can make it more vulnerable to knocks. Clean it with lukewarm water and a soft cloth, and avoid ultrasonic and steam cleaners, which can damage the stone or its treatment.

Color matters most: the most sought-after emeralds are a vivid, slightly bluish green that is neither too light nor too dark. Look at the stone in daylight and indoor light, and favor even color over perfect clarity. The emerald cut, a rectangle with cut corners, suits this stone well: the cut corners help protect it, and the long step facets show its color.

For a ring worn every day, a bezel or prongs that protect the corners guard the stone against knocks. Emeralds also suit earrings and pendants, where they are less exposed. Take emerald rings off for housework and exercise, and ask a jeweler before any cleaning beyond a soft cloth. A jeweler can also refresh an emerald’s oil treatment if its fissures become more visible over time.

title: Gemstone Guide
excerpt: Color, clarity, hardness and treatments: what to look for when choosing a colored gemstone.
subtitle: Color, clarity, hardness and treatments, and what to look for in each.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: With colored gemstones, color matters most. Gemologists describe it by hue, the color itself; tone, how light or dark it is; and saturation, how intense it is. Evenly distributed, vivid color is generally most prized, but the best color is the one you love.

The Mohs scale ranks resistance to scratching from 1 to 10. Diamond is 10, sapphire and ruby are 9, and emerald is 7.5 to 8. For a ring worn every day, harder stones resist scratches better; softer stones suit pendants and earrings, or rings worn with care.

Many gemstones are treated to improve their color or clarity. Heating sapphires and oiling emeralds are common and widely accepted; any treatment should be disclosed, and it can affect how a stone should be cleaned.

Colored gemstones are judged by eye rather than on a fixed clarity scale. Some, such as aquamarine and topaz, are usually very clean; others, such as emerald, almost always show inclusions, and these are accepted as part of the stone. Look for a gemstone without inclusions that reach its surface or make it look cloudy.

Colored gemstones are often cut to keep as much weight and color as possible, so their proportions vary more than a diamond’s. A well-cut stone shows even color, without a dull, see-through patch in the center, called a window. Ovals and cushions are popular shapes for colored gemstones. Choose the shape you like, then judge the color and life of the stone itself.

title: Jewelry Care
excerpt: Cleaning, storing and traveling with fine jewelry, so every piece keeps its shine for years.
subtitle: Cleaning, storing and traveling with fine jewelry.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Most gold and diamond jewelry can be cleaned in warm water with a drop of mild soap and a soft brush. Softer and treated gemstones, pearls and emeralds among them, need only a damp cloth. Avoid harsh chemicals, and check before using an ultrasonic cleaner.
Keep pieces in separate pouches or lined compartments so they don’t scratch or tangle. Fasten chains before you put them away, and store pearls flat.
Pack jewelry in a small padded case in your carry-on, with chains fastened and rings in their own slots, and keep the pieces you wear every day to a few favorites.

Chlorine, bleach and many household cleaners can discolor or weaken gold alloys and damage softer gemstones, so take jewelry off before swimming or cleaning. Perfume, hairspray and lotion leave a film that dulls stones: put them on before your jewelry, not after.

Every few months, look closely at prongs, clasps and earring backs. A prong that catches on fabric, a clasp that no longer closes firmly or a stone that moves when you tap the piece gently are all signs that a jeweler should take a look.

Gold-plated jewelry has a thin layer of gold over another metal; vermeil is gold over sterling silver. Wipe it with a soft, dry cloth rather than washing it, and keep it away from water and creams, so the layer lasts longer. When the gold wears thin, a jeweler can often replate the piece.

title: Lab-Grown and Natural Diamonds Compared
excerpt: Both are real diamonds. How they differ in origin, how they are graded, and how to choose between them.
subtitle: Both are real diamonds: how they differ in origin, and how they are graded.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: Lab-grown diamonds are diamonds. They have the same chemical composition, crystal structure, hardness and optical properties as diamonds formed in the earth, and they look the same to the eye. Telling them apart takes specialized laboratory instruments.

The difference is origin. Natural diamonds formed deep in the earth over a very long time; lab-grown diamonds are grown in a laboratory by high pressure, high temperature (HPHT) or chemical vapor deposition (CVD) processes that recreate those conditions. Grading reports for both state the origin, and some laboratories describe a lab-grown diamond’s quality on a different scale from a natural one’s, so check which scale a report uses.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.caption: Lab-grown or natural, cut, color, clarity and carat weight decide how a diamond looks.

body.text: Decide what matters most to you: a stone that formed naturally, or the size and quality you want. Compare both at a similar size and quality, and choose the one you love.

You can’t tell a lab-grown diamond from a natural one by looking. Grading laboratories identify the origin with specialized instruments and state it on the report, and many diamonds carry a small laser inscription on the girdle with the report number. Ask for the report, check that its number matches the inscription, and keep it with your other records.
Lab-grown and natural diamonds are equally hard and are cleaned and cared for the same way: warm water, a drop of mild soap and a soft brush, with a jeweler’s check of the setting from time to time.

title: Choosing a Metal for Everyday Wear
excerpt: Yellow, white and rose gold, and platinum: how each looks, wears and is cared for over the years.
subtitle: Yellow, white and rose gold, and platinum: how each looks and wears.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: Pure gold is too soft for everyday jewelry, so it is alloyed with other metals. The karat says how much gold the alloy holds, and 18K holds more than 14K. 14K is a little harder and more resistant to scratches, while 18K has a richer color. Yellow gold keeps its color naturally, rose gold takes its warm tone from copper, and white gold is usually plated with rhodium for a bright white finish that can be renewed over time.

Platinum is naturally white, dense and durable. Rather than wearing away, it tends to develop a soft satin patina with wear, which can be polished back to a shine. It feels heavier on the hand than gold.

Choose the metal for your engagement ring and wedding band together, and think about the jewelry you already wear every day. Mixing metals is a style choice too: a yellow gold band beside a platinum ring can look deliberate and modern.

Some people react to nickel, which is used in some white gold alloys. If you have sensitive skin, ask for a nickel-free alloy, or ask about platinum, which is often recommended for sensitive skin. The rhodium plating on white gold also keeps the alloy from touching the skin until it wears thin.

Gold of every color can be polished by a jeweler to remove fine scratches. White gold may need replating with rhodium from time to time to keep its bright white finish. Platinum’s patina can be polished away or kept, as you prefer.

title: Moissanite
excerpt: A brilliant lab-created gemstone: how moissanite compares with diamond in look, hardness and fire.
subtitle: A brilliant lab-created gemstone, and how it compares with diamond.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: Moissanite is silicon carbide, a mineral that is extremely rare in nature. The moissanite used in jewelry is created in a laboratory. It is a gemstone in its own right, not a diamond and not an imitation of one.

Moissanite is about 9.25 on the Mohs scale, very hard and well suited to everyday wear. It has more dispersion than diamond, so it shows more colorful flashes of fire, especially in sunlight. Some people love that rainbow sparkle; others prefer the white brilliance of a diamond.

Clean moissanite as you would a diamond: warm, soapy water and a soft brush, then rinse and dry. It is hard enough for a ring worn every day, but have the setting checked from time to time, as you would for any ring.

Most moissanite for jewelry is made colorless or near colorless and is usually very clean, with few visible inclusions. Descriptions of its color vary from seller to seller, so compare stones in daylight before you choose.

Moissanite is lighter than diamond, so a moissanite the same size as a diamond weighs less. It is usually described by its size in millimeters rather than by carat weight; compare stones by their diameter.

Moissanite is doubly refractive: looking into it at an angle, you may see the facet edges doubled. Simple diamond testers that measure heat can mistake it for diamond, so jewelers use testers that also measure electrical conductivity. The seller’s paperwork should say clearly that the stone is moissanite.

title: Pearl Guide
excerpt: Luster, surface, shape and size: how pearls are judged, the main types, and how to care for them.
subtitle: How pearls are judged, the main types, and how to care for them.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring and a band

body.text: Luster, the sharp glow reflected from a pearl’s surface, is the first thing to look at. Look too at the surface, for spots and blemishes; the shape, from perfectly round to baroque; the size; and, in a strand, how well the pearls match.

Akoya pearls are known for their bright luster and round shapes. Freshwater pearls come in many shapes and soft colors. South Sea pearls are larger, in white and golden tones, and Tahitian pearls are naturally dark, from gray to peacock green.

Pearls are soft, so put them on last, after perfume and makeup, and take them off first. Wipe them with a soft cloth after wearing, store them flat and apart from harder jewelry, and have strands restrung when the silk loosens.

Most pearls sold today are cultured: a pearl farmer places a small bead or piece of tissue inside a mollusk, which coats it in layers of nacre. Natural pearls, formed without help, are very rare. Both are real pearls. Imitation pearls are made of glass or plastic with a pearly coating, and feel smooth rather than slightly gritty when rubbed gently against a tooth.

Pearls look their best when worn often. A single strand that sits just below the collarbone is a versatile choice, and pearl studs are easy to wear every day. Store pearls in a soft pouch rather than an airtight bag, which can dry them out, and keep them away from harder jewelry that could scratch them.

title: Caring for Your Rings
excerpt: Simple habits that keep rings bright and secure, from cleaning at home to knowing when to see a jeweler.
subtitle: Simple habits that keep rings bright and secure.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Soak rings for a few minutes in warm water with a little mild dish soap, then brush gently with a soft toothbrush, paying attention to the back of the stone where lotion and dust collect. Rinse in a bowl rather than over an open drain, and dry with a lint-free cloth.

Take rings off for heavy work, the gym, gardening and cleaning with household chemicals, and before swimming, since chlorine can harm gold alloys over time. Put them on after lotions and perfume. Store each ring separately so harder stones don’t scratch softer metals.
Prongs wear and can bend with daily use. Have a jeweler check settings periodically, and sooner if a stone ever feels loose or a prong catches on fabric.

When you take rings off, put them somewhere safe and consistent, such as a ring dish away from sinks and drains, or a lined box with separate slots. Diamonds can scratch other diamonds and softer gemstones, so keep rings from touching one another in a drawer or bag.

A quick clean every week or two keeps a diamond bright, since lotion and everyday oils collect behind the stone and dull its sparkle. A professional clean and check once or twice a year is a good habit for rings worn every day. Ultrasonic cleaners suit many diamond rings, but not every gemstone or setting, so ask a jeweler before using one. Steam cleaners are best left to a jeweler.

title: Finding the Right Ring Size at Home
excerpt: Simple ways to measure a ring size at home, and the details that make a ring fit comfortably all day.
subtitle: Simple ways to measure at home, and the details that make a ring fit well.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring and a band

body.text: The most reliable way is to measure a ring that already fits the same finger: measure its inside diameter in millimeters and compare it with a ring size chart. Without a ring, wrap a strip of paper around the base of the finger, mark where it overlaps, and measure the length against a chart. Thread and string stretch, so paper gives a truer reading.
Fingers are slightly larger at the end of the day and in warm weather, and smaller when cold. Measure at a comfortable room temperature, ideally a couple of times on different days.

A ring should slide over the knuckle with a little resistance and sit snugly without pinching. If your knuckle is much wider than the base of your finger, choose the size that passes the knuckle. Wide bands fit more snugly than narrow ones, so you may want a quarter or half size larger for a wide band.

If the ring is a surprise, borrow a ring the wearer already wears on that finger, and measure it or trace its inside edge on paper. If that isn’t possible, a slightly larger size is the safer choice, since most rings are easier to make smaller than larger.

Fingers change over time and with the seasons. Most plain and solitaire rings can be resized by a jeweler. Rings set with stones all the way around, tension settings and some patterned or engraved bands are difficult or impossible to resize, so it is worth getting the size right for those from the start.

title: Sapphires
excerpt: Blue and far beyond: the colors, durability and care of sapphires for everyday rings.
subtitle: Blue and far beyond: color, durability and care.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring and a band

body.text: Sapphire is the mineral corundum. Blue is its best-known color, but sapphires also come in pink, yellow, orange, purple, green and white; red corundum is called ruby. Sapphires in colors other than blue are often called fancy sapphires.

At 9 on the Mohs scale, sapphire is one of the hardest gemstones, which makes it a durable choice for engagement rings. Many sapphires are heated to improve their color and clarity, a common and stable treatment.
Clean sapphires with warm, soapy water and a soft brush. They are durable, but a hard knock can still chip any gemstone, so take rings off for heavy work.

Color comes first: look for a sapphire whose color is even and stays rich in both daylight and indoor light. Some sapphires show different shades from different angles, and a good cut places the best color face up. Clarity is judged by eye, and fine, silky inclusions are common; they can even soften the color pleasantly. Ask whether the stone has been treated, and how, since that can affect its care.

Because sapphire is so hard, it can be set in the same styles as a diamond: a solitaire, a halo of diamonds around it, or three stones in a row. White gold and platinum suit blue sapphires, while yellow and rose gold flatter pink and yellow ones. A sapphire’s color can look different in each metal, so try a few before you decide.

title: Engagement Ring Settings
excerpt: Solitaire, halo, pavé, bezel or side stones: how each setting frames the center stone and wears day to day.
subtitle: How each setting frames the center stone, and how it wears day to day.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Prongs are small metal claws that grip the stone, letting in the most light; four prongs show more of the diamond, six hold it more securely. A bezel surrounds the stone with a thin rim of metal, which protects its edge and suits an active life.

A solitaire sets one stone on a plain band and puts all the attention on it. A halo circles the center stone with smaller diamonds, adding sparkle and making it look larger. Pavé lines the band with small diamonds. Side-stone and three-stone settings flank the center stone with accent stones.

High settings show off the stone but can catch on clothing; lower settings and bezels sit closer to the hand. Pavé and halo settings have many small stones, so have them checked by a jeweler from time to time. Think about how you use your hands before you decide.

If you plan to wear a wedding band beside your engagement ring, check how the two will sit together. A low setting or a halo that overhangs the shank may need a curved or notched band to sit flush. Try the two rings together before you choose.

Prongs can be rounded, pointed like claws, or flat. Rounded prongs are smooth and comfortable; claw prongs are tapered and look delicate; V-shaped prongs protect the points of pear, marquise and princess shapes; double prongs add security and a slightly different look.

title: The 4Cs of Diamonds
excerpt: Cut, color, clarity and carat weight: what each grade means, which ones you will notice, and how to balance them.
subtitle: Cut, color, clarity and carat weight, and how to balance them for the diamond you want.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: Cut describes how well a diamond’s facets are proportioned, aligned and polished, and so how it handles light. It is the only one of the 4Cs shaped entirely by the cutter. For round brilliant diamonds, the Gemological Institute of America (GIA) grades cut from Excellent to Poor, looking at proportions, symmetry and polish together. Two diamonds with the same color, clarity and weight can look very different because of cut alone.

A well-cut diamond returns light that enters through the top back out through the top, so the stone looks bright from edge to edge. If the pavilion is too deep, light escapes through the sides and the center can look dark; if it is too shallow, light leaks out through the bottom and the stone can look glassy. Some laboratories and retailers call the best-performing proportions “ideal”. On a GIA report, the top cut grade for a round diamond is Excellent.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings set with diamonds

body.caption: Cut decides how brightly a diamond returns light, whatever its size.

body.text: Three effects make up a diamond’s sparkle. Brilliance is the white light reflected back to your eye. Dispersion, often called fire, is that light split into flashes of color. Scintillation is the pattern of light and dark flashes you see when the diamond, the light or you move. A well-cut stone balances all three. Look at a diamond in more than one kind of light, not only under bright spotlights, to see how it really performs.

Diamond color grading measures how close a white diamond is to having no color at all. GIA grades it on a scale from D, colorless, to Z, light yellow or brown, by comparing each diamond face down against master stones under controlled light. The differences between neighboring grades are subtle, and many are hard to see once the diamond is face up and set in a ring.

D, E and F are the colorless grades. D is the highest; E and F show only traces of color that a trained grader can detect side by side with master stones. Colorless diamonds pair naturally with white gold and platinum, which do nothing to warm the stone.

image.alt: A colorless round diamond
A near colorless round diamond with a hint of warmth
A round diamond with a faint yellow tint

body.text: G, H, I and J are near colorless. Face up and set, most of these diamonds look white to the eye, with any warmth showing mainly when you compare them with higher grades. In yellow or rose gold, which reflect warm tones into the stone, a near colorless diamond can look just as white as a colorless one once it is set.

Clarity describes inclusions inside a diamond and blemishes on its surface, small marks that most diamonds form as they grow. GIA grades clarity under 10x magnification, from Flawless to Included, by the size, number, position and visibility of these characteristics.

For most people the aim is an eye-clean diamond: one whose inclusions you can’t see without magnification at a normal viewing distance. Many VS2 and SI1 diamonds are eye-clean, but each stone is different, so look at the diamond itself rather than the grade alone. Step-cut shapes such as emerald and Asscher, with their open, mirror-like facets, show inclusions more readily than brilliant cuts, so a higher clarity grade can be worth it there.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

options.label: SI2
options.description: Slightly included: inclusions are noticeable under 10x magnification and may be visible to the eye.

options.label: SI1
options.description: Slightly included: inclusions are noticeable under 10x magnification; many stones look clean to the eye.

options.label: VS2

options.label: VVS2

options.label: VVS1

options.label: FL

body.text: Carat is a unit of weight, not size: one carat weighs 0.2 grams, and each carat divides into 100 points, so a 75-point diamond weighs 0.75 carats. Because weight is spread differently by each shape and cut, two diamonds of the same weight can look different in size.

What you see on the hand is the diamond’s face-up spread, its diameter or length and width. A well-cut stone puts its weight where it shows, while a deeply cut one can hide weight below the girdle. Elongated shapes such as oval, marquise and pear tend to look larger than a round diamond of the same weight. Choose a few weights below to see the approximate diameter of a well-cut round diamond.

body.text: Start with cut, since it does the most for a diamond’s sparkle. Then choose the lowest color and clarity grades that still look white and clean to your eye in the setting you love: near colorless and eye-clean grades often give the best balance. Finally, choose the weight. Diamonds just under a whole or half carat look almost the same as those right at it, so a 0.90 carat stone can be a sensible alternative to a full carat. Always ask for a grading report from an independent laboratory, and compare diamonds side by side when you can.

title: Wedding Band Guide
excerpt: Widths, profiles and finishes, and how to choose a band that sits well beside your engagement ring.
subtitle: Widths, profiles and finishes, and choosing a band to sit beside your ring.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring and a band

body.text: Wedding bands range from slim, delicate widths to bold, wide ones. A flat profile has straight edges; a domed or court profile is rounded on top, and a comfort-fit band is also rounded inside so it slides on easily and feels softer on the finger. A comfort-fit band can feel a little looser than a standard one of the same size, so try on the profile you plan to wear.

If your engagement ring has a low setting, a straight band can sit flush beside it. A halo or a setting that sits low over the band may need a curved or notched band to sit close. Try the two rings together, and choose the same metal for a matched look or a contrast for a modern stack.
Polished bands shine; brushed and hammered finishes soften the look and hide fine scratches. Most finishes can be renewed by a jeweler.
Matching your band’s metal to your engagement ring keeps the pair looking like a set. Rings worn side by side rub where they touch, whatever the metal, so have both checked from time to time.

A plain band is simple to wear and care for, and easy to resize, and it suits almost any engagement ring. A pavé or channel-set band adds sparkle, but bands set with diamonds all the way around are hard to resize, so a band with diamonds across the top only can be a practical choice.

title: Amara & James
excerpt: A pear-cut diamond on a slim band, chosen together.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Amara and James decided early on that they would choose the ring together. They spent a few weekends trying shapes on, and kept coming back to the pear.
Its outline looked longer and slimmer on Amara’s hand, and it suited the simple jewelry she wears every day.
They set the pear on a slim band, so the stone leads and nothing competes with it. A prong over the point protects it from knocks, which mattered for a ring worn every day.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

cells: Pear-cut diamond on a slim band

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: A pear-cut diamond on a slim band is a quiet, lasting choice. If you choose a pear, look for even brightness from the point to the rounded end, and a prong that guards the point.

featuredImage.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

title: Grace & Tom
excerpt: Matching wedding bands in white gold.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Grace and Tom wanted wedding bands that looked like a pair, even though their hands and tastes are different.
They chose the same white gold and the same polished finish, in two widths: a slimmer band for Grace and a wider one for Tom.
Matching the metal and finish made the two bands read as a set, while choosing each width separately let each band suit the hand that wears it.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring
A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: Matching bands don’t have to be identical. The same metal and finish make a pair; the width can follow each hand.

featuredImage.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

title: Lena & Omar
excerpt: A surprise proposal with a ring designed in secret.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Omar wanted the proposal to be a complete surprise, so he designed Lena’s ring without her knowing, starting from the jewelry she already wore and loved.
He borrowed a ring she wore on the same finger to get the size right, and returned it before she noticed it was gone.
He chose a setting first, then the center stone, keeping the style close to Lena’s everyday pieces so the ring would feel like hers from the first day.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

cells: A setting and center stone chosen separately

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: If you design a ring as a surprise, start from the jewelry they already wear: it tells you their metal, their style and, with a borrowed ring, their size.

featuredImage.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

title: Nia & Marcus
excerpt: Stacked bands in yellow gold, one for every year.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

hero.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: Nia and Marcus started with a plain yellow gold wedding band. On each anniversary since, they have added another band to the stack.
Each one is a little different, a plain band one year and a band with small diamonds the next, so the stack tells their story as it grows.
Keeping every band in yellow gold holds the stack together, while the changes in width and texture make each year easy to pick out.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

cells: Plain and diamond bands, added one at a time

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: A stack that grows over the years works best when the bands share one metal. Slim bands leave room to add more, and a mix of plain and diamond bands keeps it interesting.

featuredImage.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

title: Priya & Sam
excerpt: An emerald and diamond stack for their anniversary.

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

hero.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: For their anniversary, Priya and Sam added color to Priya’s rings: an emerald band to sit between her diamond bands.
Green has always been Priya’s favorite color, and the emerald brings it into the rings she wears every day.
The emerald sits between two diamond bands, which frame its color and protect it from knocks, since emerald is softer than diamond.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

cells: One on either side of the emerald

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: A colored stone between diamond bands is a simple way to wear color every day. With softer stones such as emerald, bands on either side help protect it.

featuredImage.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

title: Sofia & Daniel
excerpt: A cushion-cut diamond with a hidden halo.

image.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

hero.alt: Crossed arms, one hand wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

body.text: Sofia wanted a ring with a soft, rounded outline, and Daniel wanted a little sparkle that only she would notice. A cushion cut with a hidden halo gave them both.
The cushion’s rounded corners and broad facets have a gentle, old-fashioned glow that Sofia loved from the start.
A hidden halo sets a row of small diamonds under the center stone, where it shows from the side rather than from above. Face up, the cushion stands alone; from the side, the halo catches the light.

image.alt: A woman with her hand over one eye, wearing a pear-shaped diamond ring

cells: Cushion-cut diamond with a hidden halo

image.alt: A hand wearing several stacked gold rings

body.text: A hidden halo adds sparkle without changing the look of the center stone from above. It suits anyone who wants a classic solitaire with a detail of their own.
